title: Range XOR Queries with Subarray Reversals
statement:
You are given an integer array `nums` and a list `queries` that is applied to `nums` one query after another. Each query is a triple whose first entry is its type:

- `[1, index, value]`: replace `nums[index]` with `value`.
- `[2, left, right]`: compute the bitwise XOR of `nums[left], nums[left + 1], ..., nums[right]` and record it.
- `[3, left, right]`: reverse the segment `nums[left..right]` (both ends included) in place.

Positions always refer to the array as it stands after all earlier queries. Return the recorded XOR values in the order their type-2 queries appear (an empty array if there are none).
constraints: For type 1: 0 <= index < nums.length and 0 <= value <= 10^9
For types 2 and 3: 0 <= left <= right < nums.length
notes:
## Intuition

Replaying the queries on a plain array is simple, but one reversal or range XOR can touch the whole array: O(n · q) work, about 10^10 at the limits. Keep the array in an **implicit treap** instead: a binary tree whose in-order traversal is the array, balanced by random heap priorities, where each node stores its subtree's `size` and XOR `total`. Two splits cut any segment out as its own tree, whose root answers for the segment, and two merges glue it back. A reversal is only a `flipped` flag, applied to the children when a later split or merge passes through.

## Approach

1. `refresh(node)` recomputes `size` and `total` from the children; `pushDown(node)` applies a pending reversal by swapping the children and toggling their flags.
2. `split(node, count)` returns `[front, back]` with the first `count` elements in `front`. It recurses into the left subtree when that holds at least `count` elements, otherwise into the right one for the remaining `count - sizeOf(node.left) - 1`.
3. `merge(front, back)` keeps the higher-priority root on top and merges the other tree into its inner side.
4. Merging one node per value of `nums`, in order, builds `root`.
5. Each query splits twice to isolate positions `left..right` as `middle` (an update uses `left = right = index`). Type 1 writes the value into that single node, type 2 records `middle.total`, type 3 toggles `middle.flipped`. Then `before`, `middle` and `after` are merged back.

## Example 1, step by step

`nums = [1,2,3,4,5]`. Query `[2,1,3]` splits into `[1]`, `[2,3,4]` and `[5]` and records `2 ^ 3 ^ 4 = 5`. Query `[1,2,10]` isolates position 2 and sets it to 10: `[1,2,10,4,5]`. Query `[3,0,4]` flips the whole tree, which now reads `[5,4,10,2,1]`. Query `[2,0,4]` records `5 ^ 4 ^ 10 ^ 2 ^ 1 = 8`. The answer is `[5, 8]`.

## Complexity

- Time: O((n + q) log n) expected: n merges to build, then two splits and two merges per query, each along a path of expected depth O(log n).
- Space: O(n) for the nodes, plus O(log n) expected recursion depth.

## Pitfalls

- Call `pushDown` before reading a node's children in `split` and `merge`; otherwise `sizeOf(node.left)` counts the wrong side.
- After relinking a child, call `refresh`, or sizes and totals go stale.
- A reversal leaves its own range's XOR unchanged, but later queries depend on the order it creates, so it cannot be skipped.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `root` | the treap holding the current array |
| `value`, `total`, `size` | a node's own value, its subtree's XOR and its subtree's node count |
| `priority` | random key that keeps the tree balanced |
| `flipped` | a reversal of this subtree not yet passed to its children |
| `front`, `back` | the two trees that `split` returns and `merge` joins |
| `before`, `middle`, `after` | the parts before, inside and after the queried range |

narration.2: An empty tree (null) has size 0; otherwise read the size stored at its root.
narration.3: An empty tree adds nothing to an XOR; otherwise read the XOR stored at its root.
narration.5: A subtree holds its left subtree, the node itself and its right subtree.
narration.6: Its XOR total combines the left subtree, the node's own value and the right subtree.
narration.9: Is a reversal of this subtree still waiting to be applied?
narration.10: Reversing a subtree mirrors it, so the two children swap places...
narration.11: ...and each child's own subtree must be reversed too, so it inherits the pending flag.
narration.13: This node's reversal has now been applied.
narration.18: Splitting an empty tree gives two empty trees.
narration.19: Apply any pending reversal first, so node.left really is the earlier part.
narration.20: The left subtree already holds count elements or more, so the cut lies inside it.
narration.21: Split the left subtree; its back part stays to the left of this node.
narration.24: Everything from this node on belongs to the back tree.
narration.26: Otherwise the left subtree and this node go to the front, and the cut lies in the right subtree after the elements already taken.
narration.27: The right subtree's front part stays attached to the right of this node.
narration.33: Merging with an empty tree just returns the other tree.
narration.34: The root with the higher priority stays on top, which keeps the tree balanced.
narration.36: front stays the root, so back is merged into its right side, after all of front's elements.
narration.41: back stays the root, so front is merged into its left side, before all of back's elements.
narration.47: Each value becomes a one-element tree with a random priority.
narration.48: Appending it to the right of root builds the array in order.
narration.53: An update touches only position index; the other queries touch left..right.
narration.54: Cut off the elements before the range...
narration.55: ...then the next right - left + 1 elements: middle holds exactly the range.
narration.57: An update rewrites the single node's value...
narration.58: ...and, as it has no children, its XOR total too.
narration.60: A range query reads the XOR of the whole range straight from middle's root.
narration.62: A reversal only toggles the flag at middle's root; children are swapped later, when needed.
narration.64: Glue the three parts back together in their order.
narration.66: Return the recorded XOR values in query order.
